title: Telemedicine and Triage
answer: Symptom routing, camera-based vital signs, wearables, conversational care and mental health signals.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Symptom Triage and Routing
children.blurb: Symptom triage and routing covers automated systems that take a patient's reported symptoms, ask follow-up questions, and assign an urgency level or direct them to an appropriate care setting, such as self-care, primary care, urgent care, or emergency services.

children.name: Vital Signs from a Camera
children.blurb: Vital signs from a camera refers to software that estimates pulse rate, respiratory rate, and sometimes blood oxygen saturation from subtle color changes and motion in a person's face or chest captured by an ordinary camera.

children.name: Wearable Data in Clinical Care
children.blurb: Wearable data in clinical care covers continuous or intermittent physiological signals collected outside the clinic, such as heart rate, activity, sleep, blood oxygen, glucose, and single-lead electrocardiogram readings, and their use in remote monitoring, triage, and chronic disease management.

children.name: Conversational Care and Its Limits
children.blurb: Conversational care refers to AI systems that interact with patients through text or voice to collect symptoms, answer questions, and support triage before or instead of a human clinician.

children.name: Digital Signals of Mental Health
children.blurb: Digital signals of mental health are behavioral and physiological data collected through phones, wearables, and telehealth platforms that may indicate changes in mood, sleep, activity, speech, or social engagement.

sections.body: Telemedicine and triage covers AI that routes patients to appropriate care, estimates vital signs from video, interprets data from wearables, conducts conversational assessments, and flags possible mental health signals. In practice, symptom checkers ask structured questions and produce a suggested level of urgency, camera-based tools measure pulse and breathing rate from subtle color changes in the face, and wearable algorithms watch for irregular heart rhythms or sleep disturbances. Conversational agents collect histories and offer follow-up questions, while text and voice analysis looks for patterns associated with depression or anxiety. These are working systems in clinics, apps, and remote monitoring programs, not laboratory prototypes.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Some parts are mature and some are not. Symptom routing is widely used but still makes errors on uncommon presentations, and it cannot replace a clinician's judgment. Camera vital signs work in good lighting and still faces, but accuracy drops with movement, dark skin, or poor video quality. Wearable data is useful for continuous trends, yet false alarms and missed events remain common. Conversational care handles simple, structured interviews well, but it struggles with ambiguity, interruption, and emotional nuance. The site tracks six active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies, which shows that failures in these tools can have serious consequences. Honest limits include biased training data, narrow validation, and a lack of evidence that many tools improve outcomes.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: Symptom Triage and Routing explains how a patient's answers become a recommended level of care and where those recommendations break down. Vital Signs from a Camera covers the signal processing behind remote pulse and respiration measurement, including the conditions that make it unreliable. Wearable Data in Clinical Care looks at how continuous streams from watches and patches are turned into alerts and trends for clinicians. Conversational Care and Its Limits examines what chatbots and voice agents can and cannot do in a medical interview. Digital Signals of Mental Health describes the use of language, typing speed, and phone use patterns to infer mood or risk, along with the privacy and validity concerns that follow. Together they move from the first point of contact to long term monitoring and mental health inference.
